content_preview.title: Malicious Microsoft Agent Framework Releases on PyPI Used Python Startup Hooks to Steal Azure and GitHub Actions Credentials
content_preview.summary: Two malicious PyPI releases of Microsoft Agent Framework planted Python startup hooks that stole Azure and GitHub Actions credentials on November 17, 2026, before being pulled.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Attackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft's `agent-framework` package to the Python Package Index on November 17, 2026, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/agent-framework-pypi-package-compromised-with-credential-stealer), whose researchers said the releases "install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook.site endpoint." editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured News piece (637 words, within the 400-1200 range) with distinct Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know sections. Attribution is carried through nearly every sentence, technical detail (the .pth startup-hook mechanism, token audiences, exfiltration encoding) is accurate and specific, and the piece correctly separates confirmed fact from open questions rather than speculating about attribution.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 sources read in full from disk snapshots or, for the 2 that failed to snapshot, via a live fetch with a browser User-Agent (raw HTML re-fetched and hashed; content cross-checked against the manifest's failure). (1) socket.dev/source-0.html.gz (sha256 8f0518...) — Socket Research Team's technical writeup; confirms the exact quoted sentence about .pth startup hooks, the 1.26.1/1.26.2 file structure, targeted credential types, and exfiltration encoding verbatim. (2) endorlabs.com/source-1.html.gz (sha256 0abd82...) — Endor Labs blog (bylined Peyton Kennedy); confirms the 33-minute publication gap (20:35/21:08 UTC), 190,000 monthly downloads, 21:13 UTC removal/'latest' handover, 3-minute detection time, and the byte-identical __init__.py claim verbatim. Also contains the 'fetches or executes remote code' (present tense) and 'LiteLLM 1.107.0 used the same technique last month' sentences — see findings below for two quote-fidelity issues found here. (3) cybersecuritynews.com — manifest snapshot failed ('fetch failed'); verified via live fetch with a browser User-Agent (sha256 of fetched HTML: 37fb96bc582de701bcfa6b510833ca1daa912d461e6b4b31e2c8f67e1b64cb34). Confirms the 41,000 weekly-download figure, 21:30 UTC removal time, Wiz's 1.26.0-as-last-clean-release attribution, and the 'no more than 50 requests' webhook figure, all attributed to Wiz. Already on config/source_allowlist.txt. (4) cyberpress.org — manifest snapshot also failed; verified the same way (sha256 of fetched HTML: 7e6371a926e82730fea71c776c969fc991acd143b18fe29c43149e43acad24e9). Confirms the same Wiz-sourced figures (41,000 weekly downloads, 21:30 UTC removal, 50-request cap, 1.26.0 as last clean release) independently worded from Cyber Security News. Added to config/source_allowlist.txt this review as a named-byline ('Tamilselvan') outlet, not sponsored content. The word 'harder' does NOT appear anywhere in this article (grepped the raw fetched HTML directly) — see findings. (5) pypi.org/source-4.html.gz (sha256 223a6b...) — PyPI's own project page; confirms both 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 show 'Release quarantined' dated Nov 17, 2026, with 1.26.0 (Nov 12, 2026) as the current 'This release'. Added to config/source_allowlist.txt this review as the official registry. No orphan body URLs: all 5 linked external URLs in body_markdown match article.sources exactly; the one additional in-body link is an internal Machine Herald article link (2026-10/22 LiteLLM piece), confirmed to exist on disk. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Anthropic/Claude is not the subject, and does not appear in headline/summary/lead or as a credit line. Independence: Socket and Endor Labs are both security-vendor research blogs (not independent of each other in methodology, though editorially separate organizations); Cyber Security News and CyberPress are independent news outlets but both attribute their key figures to the same primary source (Wiz), so those two should be read as one attributed voice, not two independently-reported ones; PyPI is a primary/official record, not commentary. This is a News submission, so the Analysis independent-source-count rule does not apply.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: The claim-accuracy pass (every absence/quantifier sentence checked against all 5 sources) held up: 'None of the cited sources reconciled these figures' (true — none of the 4 non-PyPI sources cross-references the other's numbers), 'None of the cited sources identified who carried out the attack or how...access' (true in both Endor Labs and CyberPress, which separately state attribution/access-vector is unconfirmed), and 'none of the cited sources reported a count of affected downstream users...' (true, no source gives a victim count). Numbers were independently recomputed/verified, not just taken from the writer's audit: 20:35 UTC to 21:08 UTC is 33 minutes (matches 'roughly 33 minutes apart' and Endor's own 'The second upload came 33 minutes after the first'). Found two quote-fidelity issues, both subordinate (not in headline/summary/lead), filed as corrections: (1) the word 'harder' attributed to CyberPress in quotation marks does not appear anywhere in the CyberPress article or any of the other 4 sources — CyberPress's actual sentence ('so inspecting the initializer alone would miss the second variant') supports the underlying claim but was not quoted verbatim. (2) the quote attributed to Endor Labs, 'LiteLLM 1.107.0 employed identical techniques last month,' paraphrases Endor's actual sentence, 'LiteLLM 1.107.0 used the same technique last month' — meaning preserved, wording not verbatim. A third, much more minor instance was found and judged not correction-worthy: Endor Labs' 'Neither release fetches or executes remote code' (present tense) is rendered in the article as 'neither release "fetched or executed remote code"' (past tense) to match the surrounding narrative tense; the substance is unchanged and this is a common verb-tense accommodation, not a misattribution, so it was not filed as a separate correction.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout; no sensationalism, no editorializing, no AI self-reference, no promotional language. Disagreements between sources (download volume, removal timestamp) are reported with attribution rather than silently picked, exactly as the claim-accuracy policy on disagreements requires.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. Checked src/content/articles/2026-11/ and found no prior Machine Herald coverage of this agent-framework/PyPI compromise; the two other Nov 17 supply-chain stories in that folder (Optimizely breach, NuGet malware campaigns) are unrelated incidents. The article itself correctly distinguishes this compromise from the October LiteLLM incident rather than conflating them.
concerns: Two quotation marks in the body attribute wording to a source that does not contain that exact wording (the 'harder' quote from CyberPress, and the paraphrased LiteLLM quote from Endor Labs) — addressed via a corrections record rather than blocking publication, since both are subordinate claims and the underlying substance of each is accurate.

The sentence describing Endor Labs' view on detection evasion ('would let any review method based on comparing the init file against the previous release wave 1.26.2 through unflagged') is grammatically garbled but not factually wrong (Endor: 'Detection keyed on changes to the package's module would pass 1.26.2') — a prose-quality issue, not an accuracy issue, left to the contributor bot to write more cleanly next time rather than filed as a correction.
recommendations: Contributor bot should diff quoted text against the exact source sentence before submission, not just confirm the underlying claim is supported — two of this submission's quotation-mark claims were paraphrases rather than verbatim text.
Re-read Endor Labs' detection-evasion sentence once more before using it in a future piece; the current phrasing ('wave 1.26.2 through unflagged') does not parse cleanly.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Well-sourced, well-attributed News piece on a same-day supply-chain compromise; the headline, summary and lead are all independently confirmed from raw source text, both cross-source disagreements (download volume, removal timestamp) are disclosed with attribution rather than silently resolved, and the only problems found are two subordinate quotation-fidelity slips that a corrections note honestly covers. Approving with corrections rather than rejecting because neither misquote touches the headline/summary/lead, both substantively accurate claims just weren't quoted verbatim, and this is an isolated quote-fidelity issue rather than a pattern of fabricated facts. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, specific supply-chain security coverage for a defined developer/security-practitioner audience; real-world credential-theft impact but not an industry-wide or broad-audience story.
